title: Rabbit territorial behaviour and group management
subtitle: Why rabbits fight and how to manage groups without constant injuries.
excerpt: Rabbits are social animals that live in complex hierarchical groups in the wild, but domesticated rabbits introduced to each other without care will often fight seriously enough to injure or kill. Understanding the social triggers, recognising the difference between squabbles and real fights, and knowing how to introduce rabbits correctly is essential for keeping groups of meat rabbits, Angoras, or companion rabbits together without constant management headaches.

glossaryTerms.definition: The process of introducing two or more rabbits to each other in a controlled way until they accept each other as companions and can share space without fighting. A successful bond involves mutual grooming, lying in contact, and shared resting.

Surgical removal of the reproductive organs in rabbits. Neutering significantly reduces territorial and sexual aggression in both males and females, and is the single most effective step for safe group housing. Uneutered males are incompatible with almost any grouping except a solo or bonded male-female pair.

content.text: Rabbits are not naturally peaceful with each other. Wild rabbits live in strict hierarchies, and new introductions cause conflict until rank is settled. Without enough space, resources, or a proper introduction, domestic rabbits will fight. Bites and scratches to the face or hindquarters can be severe enough to need a vet.
Neutering as a baseline
Neutering

is the most important step in reducing aggression. Unneutered bucks are territorial and fight other males. They also mount females without stopping. Unneutered does often become aggressive at 6 to 14 months, even toward familiar rabbits. For companion or Angora rabbits in a group, neuter all. For meat production, keep bucks and does separate and pair only for mating.
Group sizes and compositions
A bonded neutered pair (buck and doe, or two does) is the most stable combination.
Groups of three neutered rabbits can work but need careful introduction and more space. The lowest-ranking rabbit can be persistently excluded.
Two unneutered bucks kept together will almost always fight seriously once mature.
For meat rabbit production, does are kept singly or in litters of same-sex weaners. Bucks are kept individually except during mating.
Bonding procedure
Successful
bonding
typically takes one to four weeks. Key points:

Initial meetings on neutral ground: a space neither rabbit has lived in before, which removes territorial triggers. A bathtub, an unfamiliar room, or a pen cleaned and arranged with new items works well.
Keep first meetings short (15 to 20 minutes) and supervised, with a way to separate the rabbits quickly if a chase escalates to biting.
Expect some mounting (dominance behaviour), chasing, and circling. This is normal. A chase that results in a fight (loud thuds, biting, fur pulled out) needs immediate separation.
Gradually increase session length as the rabbits settle. Signs of progress: mutual grooming, lying near each other, eating side by side.
Once rabbits groom and rest together consistently, move them to their permanent shared space. Clean and rearrange it first so neither rabbit sees it as their territory.
Resource spacing

Even bonded pairs benefit from having two of everything: two water sources, two feeding stations, two resting platforms or hidey holes. A bonded rabbit that controls the single food bowl can exclude its partner. This is a management fix rather than a bonding failure.

A rabbit that is bonded to one partner and then loses that partner through illness or death often goes through a grief response: reduced appetite, lethargy, and changes in behaviour. Re-bonding can take longer and be harder than the original pair introduction, as the surviving rabbit is both grieving and now used to its home as a solo territory.
